notes.meaning: Solomon is now firmly settled as king over all twelve tribes of Israel. The kings after him would rule only part of the land. The chapter shows the kingdom at its high point, in the best years of his reign.

Next comes a list of Solomon's top officials. Choosing good helpers was part of his God-given wisdom, because a wise leader shares the work with the right people. Azariah, from the family of Zadok the priest, comes first. Some older commentators think the word here means he was the king's chief minister. Others take it to mean he served as priest.

Two brothers served as secretaries, writing the king's letters and records. Their father had been David's secretary. Jehoshaphat, the recorder, had also served David. Solomon wisely kept the trusted men his father had used.

Benaiah took Joab's place as head of the army. Zadok is named as priest along with Abiathar. That is surprising, because Solomon had removed Abiathar from his post. Many commentators think Abiathar kept the title and honor of priest but no longer did the work. The Geneva Notes suggest this may be a different man with the same name.

Azariah son of Nathan oversaw the twelve governors listed below. Zabud was the king's trusted adviser and close friend. Many take this Nathan to be the prophet who helped Solomon become king, so Solomon was honoring his family. Others think he was Solomon's brother Nathan, a son of David.
Ahishar ran the palace household. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor, the workers the king called up for building projects. He had held a similar job under David.

Taxes were paid in food and farm goods, not money. Solomon set up twelve governors, one for each month of the year. Each district supplied the palace for one month. That way no area was drained, and the work and the profit were spread around fairly.

Several governors are named only as "son of" someone, like Ben-hur ("son of Hur"). That was a common way to name people, perhaps because the fathers were well known. Ben-hur oversaw the hills of Ephraim, one of the most fruitful areas of the land.
Ben-deker's district was a group of towns in the territory of the tribe of Dan, west of Ephraim.
Ben-hesed's district included Socoh and the land of Hepher, likely in the lowlands of Judah. The exact place of Arubboth is not known.

Ben-abinadab oversaw the coastal area around Dor, south of Mount Carmel. He was married to Solomon's daughter Taphath. Matthew Henry notes it was better for her to marry a faithful Israelite official than a foreign prince who did not know God.

Baana's district covered the cities on the edge of the Jezreel valley, like Taanach, Megiddo and Beth-shean. It reached east to the Jordan River. He may have been a brother of Jehoshaphat the recorder.
Ben-geber ruled from Ramoth-gilead, east of the Jordan. His area held the sixty strong, walled cities once taken from King Og and named after Jair. Their gates were barred with bronze.
Ahinadab was sent to Mahanaim, an important fortified city east of the Jordan.

Ahimaaz, perhaps the son of Zadok the priest, oversaw Naphtali in the north. Like Ben-abinadab, he married one of Solomon's daughters. That suggests this list comes from the middle or later years of Solomon's reign.
Baana son of Hushai served in Asher. His father was probably Hushai, David's loyal friend and wise counselor. Solomon kept honoring the families who had been faithful to David.
Jehoshaphat oversaw Issachar, and Shimei oversaw Benjamin. Solomon did not stick strictly to the old tribal borders. He drew the districts in whatever way worked best.

Geber had the large land of Gilead, east of the Jordan, which was once ruled by kings Sihon and Og. The closing words say there was also one governor over Judah. Some think Judah, the king's home tribe, was handled apart from the twelve districts.

God had promised Abraham children "as the sand on the seashore," and now that promise was coming true. The people had plenty and lived in peace and joy. Matthew Henry sees this as good: they enjoyed God's gifts with cheerful hearts instead of hoarding them. It also gives a small picture of the joy and peace of all who follow Jesus.

differ.view: Adam Clarke and Joseph Benson read this as a warning. So much comfort and feasting made the people careless and led to moral decay, just as prosperity often does.

notes.meaning: Solomon's rule reached from the Euphrates River to the border of Egypt. The smaller kingdoms in between paid him tribute, which means regular payments of goods. David's wars had won this peace, and Solomon's wisdom kept it. Matthew Henry sees it as a picture pointing ahead to Christ, whose kingdom will reach all nations.

differ.view: Some believe this was not the full keeping of God's land promise to Abraham. The nations only paid tribute, and Israel itself still lived from Dan to Beersheba.

notes.meaning: This is how much food the palace used each day. A "cor" was a large measure, roughly 220 liters. The food fed not just the king but his whole court, officials, guards, and guests, probably many thousands of people. Matthew Henry notes that Christ does even more: he feeds his people with the bread of eternal life.

Solomon could supply all this because he ruled the whole region west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah in the north to Gaza in the south. Best of all, he had peace on every side. Some see in this a picture of Christ, the Prince of Peace.

Sitting "under your own vine and fig tree" was a well-loved way of saying people lived safely and at peace. Families no longer had to crowd into walled cities for safety. They could spread out, farm their land, and eat what they grew. Solomon did not seize people's property. The prophets later used this same picture for the Messiah's coming age.

Solomon kept many horses for chariots and riders to guard the peace. Some copies say 40,000 stalls. Many commentators think that is a copying slip for the 4,000 found in 2 Chronicles 9:25. God had told Israel's kings not to gather many horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). Some see a warning sign here. Matthew Henry felt Solomon's numbers were modest next to his neighbors'.

Each governor took his month and made sure nothing was missing for the king's table. They also delivered barley and chopped straw, the usual feed for horses, to wherever it was needed. Everyone knew his place and his job, so the large court ran without confusion. Spurgeon drew a lesson from this: each believer has a task in Christ's kingdom and should give as he is able.

Solomon's wisdom was a gift from God, given just as God had promised in answer to his prayer. "Largeness of heart" means a wide, deep mind that could take in many kinds of knowledge. Some add that he was also generous in sharing what he knew. Like sand on the shore, his understanding was too great to measure.

The peoples to the east, such as Arabians and Chaldeans, and the Egyptians were famous for their learning. Yet Solomon's wisdom was greater than all of theirs. Matthew Henry notes that knowledge God gives goes beyond what people get by their own effort.

Solomon was wiser than the best-known wise men of his day. These included Ethan and Heman, who were temple musicians and are linked with Psalms 88 and 89. "Sons of Mahol" may be a family name or may mean skilled musicians and poets. His fame spread to all the nations around.

Solomon spoke 3,000 proverbs, or wise sayings, and wrote 1,005 songs. Only part of these survive. Some of the proverbs are kept in the Bible's book of Proverbs, along with the Song of Songs and perhaps a psalm or two. Matthew Henry suggests God preserved the ones that were inspired, meaning written with the Holy Spirit's guidance.

Solomon studied nature. The great cedar and the tiny hyssop plant mark the biggest and smallest of plants, so the phrase means "every plant." He also taught about all kinds of animals. Adam Clarke calls him perhaps the world's first natural scientist and grieves that these writings are lost.

Kings sent people from many nations to hear Solomon's wisdom. The Queen of Sheba, in chapter 10, is the best-known example. Matthew Henry sees Solomon here as a picture of Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom are found. People from every nation will come to him and find rest for their souls.
